newsitem.title: USA: EU wants smooth Boeing merger probe with U.S.
newsitem.headline: EU wants smooth Boeing merger probe with U.S.

text.p: A top European Union official said Thursday he will strive to see eye-to-eye with U.S. officials as he examines issues critics have raised about the proposed Boeing Co.-McDonnell Douglas Corp. merger.

"We will do everything to come to identical views with American authorities on objections to the deal and once we have reached this then we will look into possible remedies," said Alexander Schaub, director-general for competition of the EU's executive commission.
He is to meet with U.S. officials on Friday.
"And I believe they (the Americans) will do everything also to avoid contradictory conclusions," he told reporters.

Schaub, the No. 2 man in the EU competition authority, will discuss the problems with those scrutinising the merger at the Federal Trade Commission. Such regularly scheduled meetings deal with a broad range of competition issues.

In a speech to the European Institute, Schaub also sought to reassure Americans, some of whom have been critical of the EU handling of the Boeing-McDonnell merger, which was valued at nearly $14 billion after it was announced in December.

For example, U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky said in The Hague last month that Americans want "assurances that the inquiry must be conducted on competition policy principles and not on extraneous political principles."
Some Americans have suggested the Europeans are putting concerns about the European airplane consortium, Airbus Industrie first.
During his speech, Schaub said the EU has authority over the Boeing merger and is carrying out its investigation in strict compliance with the law.
"We do not consider Boeing to be a case of extraterritorial application of EU merger control laws," he said. "The commission will scrutinise this merger under strictly legal terms."
He also replied to Americans who have charged the EU is using the proposed merger as a pretext for renegotiating an agreement on subsidies to American and European aircraft manufacturers.
"We are not prepared to politicize or take account of trade considerations" in the exploration of the merger, he said.
The merger would narrow the number of major commercial airline manufacturers from three to two and Europeans -- along with some Americans -- have cited concerns about competition.
The meetings between the FTC and Schaub come as both are moving toward deadlines.

The EU must make a final decision by July 31. The FTC must act 20 business days after Boeing and McDonnell Douglas submit all required paperwork regarding the merger, which Boeing officials said will probably happen by next week.
